title: TA9-17627
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, (the "principal claimant" ), his wife, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the "co-claimant" hereinafter called the claimant) and their child XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the minor claimant) claim to be citizens of Ethiopia and seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 Designated Representative

XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX was appointed the Designated Representative of the minor claimant on September 18, 2009. At the hearing, the principal claimant confirmed his agreement to act as his daughter's designated representative. Allegations
The principal claimant was born in XXXXX XXXXX, Ethiopia on XXXXXX, 1974. The claimant was born in XXXXX XXXXX on XXXXXX, 1977. The minor claimant was born in Paris, France on XXXXXX, 2008.

The principal claimant and the minor claimant depend upon the claim of the claimant, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX. The claimant alleges the following. The principal claimant, the claimant and the minor claimant are citizens of Ethiopia. The claimant's father, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, who resided in France for the past thirty years, was a XXXXX XXXX of an XXXXX XXXXX XXXX, the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The principal claimant and the claimant were married XXXXX 2005. In XXXX 2005 the claimant moved to France to take up the position of XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (XXXXX) headquarters in Paris, France. The claimant lived with her father in Paris. The principal claimant joined the claimant in Paris the following year. Soon after the claimant arrived in Paris in 2005, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX which caused many changes in the Ethiopian staff in Paris at that time. Shortly after, senior staff came to know that the claimant was the daughter of XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The matter was reported to the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and questions were asked regarding the recruitment of the claimant to a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

At times, the claimant was required to work at the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris when they were short staffed. The claimant was requested to work to gain support for the XXXXX XXXXX among the Ethiopians working at the XXXXX Headquarters. She was unwilling to promote the political ideology of the XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant was accused of assisting her father in his political writing. It was discovered that her husband had travelled to Ethiopia in 2009 with XXXXX XXXX XXXXX political writings. In 2009, the claimant learned that her name, her husband's name and her father's name were on a list compiled by the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris. The list named XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

The claimant was accused of not convincing XXXXX to release funds for Ethiopian projects. Her inaction was blamed on her political beliefs. She received verbal abuse, warnings and intimidation in regard to this matter each time she XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

The claimant received a letter dated XXXX, 2009 from the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris informing her that her employment was terminated and she was instructed to travel to Ethiopia and report to the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX by XXXXX, 2009.

The claimant, principal claimant and minor claimant travelled to Canada on a holiday. They arrived in Canada on XXXXX, 2009. While on holiday, the claimant learned, through a friend of a friend who works at the XXXXX XXXXX office in XXXXX XXXXX, that, upon her return to Ethiopia, the claimant would be interrogated about her father's political activities. She understood that the interrogation would include torture and imprisonment. She heard from her family in Ethiopia that they had received telephone calls from unknown individuals requesting information on the claimant's return to Ethiopia.
The claimant, principal claimant and minor claimant made claims for refugee protection on September 1, 2009.
Subsequent to their arrival in Canada, the principal claimant's and claimant's son, XXXXX XXXXX, was born on XXXXX, 2010. The claimant's father, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, died in early XXXXX, 2010.

The panel finds that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, (the "principal claimant" ), his wife, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the claimant) and their child, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX (the minor claimant), are not Convention refugees pursuant to s. 96 of the IRPA, nor are they persons in need of protection, pursuant to s. 97(1) of IRPA.
The issues in this hearing were: * Credibility * Failure to claim in France Identity

The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the principal claimant is who he says he is and that he is a citizen of Ethiopia. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is who she says she is and that she is a citizen of Ethiopia. In support of their identities, each provided a copy of their Ethiopian passport2 and birth certificate.3

The minor claimant was born in Paris, France. A copy of her birth certificate was provided to the panel.4 She was born to foreign parents and left France before the age of two years. The claimant provided a copy of a document, 'Council of Europe, France, Legislative provisions Concerning Nationality',5 which states: "Since 1 September 1998 children born in France to foreign parents born abroad acquire French nationality ipso jure when they reach the age of majority or may themselves apply for French nationality as of 16 years of age; alternately, their legal representative may lodge an application with their consent once they have reached the age of 13."

The panel therefore finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the minor claimant is a citizen of Ethiopia. In support of her identity, a copy of her passport6 was provided as well as her birth certificate previously mentioned. Credibility The Claimant

The sworn testimony of the claimant is presumed to be truthful unless there is valid reason to doubt its truthfulness.7 Nonetheless, the panel finds that the claimant has failed to advance her claim with evidence that is consistent or credible. The panel is aware that none of the credibility concerns raised here may be sufficient, each on its own, to negate this claim. However, the cumulative effect of all of them is that the panel does not have sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence upon which to base a determination that the claimant is a Convention refugee. As the Court of Appeal in Sheikh,8 MacGuigan, J.A. held: even without disbelieving every word [a claimant] has uttered, a ... panel may reasonably find him so lacking in credibility that it concludes that there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim ... In other words, a general finding of a lack of credibility on the part of the applicant may concurrently extend to all relevant information emanating from his testimony.

A crucial aspect of the claimant's claim is that some months after she arrived in France in 2005, new senior staff appeared and it was only then that her relationship with her father became known and, thus, her troubles with those working for the XXXXX XXXXX began. The panel is not persuaded that the relationship between the claimant and her father, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, was a reason for XXXXX XXXXX to require her to return to Ethiopia from Paris in 2009. The panel is guided by the words of Mr. Justice Mahoney in Orelien9 wherein he stated: It seems to me one cannot be satisfied the evidence is credible or trustworthy unless satisfied that it is probably so, not just possibly so.

The panel is not persuaded that XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX's political activities were of such interest to the Ethiopian authorities as to wish to persecute his daughter, the claimant. The panel's reasons follow. * The claimant testified that XXXXX XXXX XXXXX had worked for the XXXXX XXXXX and was involved in XXXXX XXXXX. She provided a copy of a document 'XXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX'10 which lists the XXXX XXXX in Ethiopia in XXXX; XXXXX XXXX XXXXX is listed as XXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (XXX) and 'XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX'. A document provided by the claimant entitled 'Col. Asrat Bogale passed away'11 states that the Colonel left Ethiopia when the Derg military came to power in the 1970s by hijacking an airplane; he was forced to land in Djibouti, jailed for two years and then was given political asylum by the French government. The document also states that he later helped to form the Ethiopian National United Front (ENUF). Other documents provided by the claimant indicate that the Colonel has waged a political campaign from outside Ethiopia for over thirty years.12 Colonel Bogale left Ethiopia in 1977 when the Derg regime was in power; the Derg regime lost power in 1991 when the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) came to power.13 The claimant testified that her father left Ethiopia before she was born. Thus, by 2005, Colonel Bogale had been out of Ethiopia for more than thirty-five years. The EDU party of which Colonel Bogale was a leader in 1995 is one of eighty-six Ethiopian political parties listed in one of the documents referred to above.14 In the article 'Col. Asrat Bogale passed away'15 the ENUF party that the he later helped to form is described as a "clandestine group". The ENUF party is not found in the list of Ethiopian political parties in the 'Annex F: List of registered political parties' in the United Kingdom (UK), 18 January 2008, Home Office XXXX.16 The claimant testified that her father is XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXX. She provided a copy of a letter17 from the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The letter is a brief acknowledgement of a letter XXXXX XXXXX wrote to the president of France. There is no persuasive evidence in the letter that XXXXX XXXXX is well known to the president of France or other French authorities. The panel believes that the claimant's father, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, XXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. * The claimant, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX [panel's emphasis], carries her father's name, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX [panel's emphasis]. The claimant testified that she applied for the position with XXXXX through the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXX. She testified that she did not know if at that time a thorough check was done on her background. The panel finds it unreasonable that the XXXXXX XXXXXX were not aware of the claimant's relationship with her father when she was XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in Paris. The documentary evidence provided by the claimant implies that her father was a XXXXXXXXX XXXXX. The independent documentary evidence indicates that the Ethiopian government keeps excessive control of its citizens18 and particularly those in opposition.19 Documentary evidence states that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs screens applications for international NGOs and submits a recommendation whether to approve or deny registration.20 While this information is not in regards to Ethiopians representing their government abroad it implies that the Minister of Foreign Affairs is aware of and involved in organizations, such as UNESCO, that affect international relationships. The panel believes that it is probable that the Ethiopian authorities knew of the claimant's relationship to her father before she went to France and, nevertheless, allowed her to travel and work there. If, however, this is not the case and, as the claimant alleges, her relationship to her father was discovered in late 2005, the panel observes that the claimant was permitted to remain in France for more than two and a half years after this discovery. The panel does not believe that the claimant would have been allowed to work in France or, as the case may be, remain in France if her father were considered a serious opponent to the Ethiopian government. Documentary evidence suggests that those in opposition to the government or family members of those in opposition are harshly treated; this includes job discrimination and dismissal from employment.21 * The claimant provided no evidence that she or her mother or sister suffered any harm at the hands of the Ethiopian authorities while she was growing up. The claimant was able to attend college and university in XXXXX XXXXX 22 and she had gainful employment23 following her studies. She was able to leave the country to work in France. The claimant testified that her mother was allowed to leave the country in 2010 to travel to France when XXXXX XXXXX became ill; the claimant testified that her mother remains in France. The panel believes that this would not have been the case if XXXXX XXXXX were considered a serious opponent of the XXXXX authorities. The Response to Information Request ETH103318.FE24 states that according to the Deputy Director of Amnesty International's Africa program, people may have been detained solely for their family ties to people who have expressed political opposition to the government. The Response to Information Request ETH102699.E25 states that there are several examples of members of opposition groups and relatives of members who have been ill-treated for being suspected of supporting the opposition. Relatives of members of the opposition are treated as enemy of the government of Ethiopia; they are subjected to treatment such as job discrimination, unlawful dismissal, refusal of business licence applications or loss of existing business licences, and denial of university admission or grants. The panel does not believe that the claimant and her family would have lived without incident in Ethiopia if XXXXX XXXXX were XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXX XXXXX.

The panel is not persuaded that the claimant was to be returned to Ethiopia to face persecution. The panel has considered the claimant's testimony and the documentary evidence. The claimant testified that she received a letter, dated XXXXX, 2009, from the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris reprimanding her for her negligence in XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She provided a copy of this document and a translation.26 The claimant testified that she was informed on XXXX, 2009 by letter from the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris that her services were no longer required and she was to return to Ethiopia no later than XXXXX, 2009. The claimant provided a copy of this letter and a translation.27 The independent documentary evidence does not support the claimant's allegation that she would face persecution in Ethiopia upon return from her XXXXX XXXXX in Paris. The Response to Information Request ETH102458.E 28 focuses specifically on Ethiopians working for the government at embassies outside the country. The Response29 states that staff from various Ethiopian embassies left their posts for refusing to implement plans to influence the Ethiopian diaspora who were in opposition to the Ethiopian government. The Response30 also indicates that Ethiopian diplomats were recalled and suspended for perceived disloyalty to their government. Thus, the panel infers that people in positions such as the claimant's chose to leave the embassies and only diplomats were recalled. There is no indication that any of these people faced persecution upon return to Ethiopia. The Response31 deals specifically with people working in Ethiopian embassies who returned to Ethiopia because they did not agree with the government. Since there is a plethora of information in other documentary evidence regarding the harsh treatment meted out by the Ethiopian authorities to those who oppose the government32 the panel would expect information in the Response regarding the harsh treatment of people in the Ethiopian embassies who opposed the government if such were the case. There is no such evidence. The panel is guided by the decision in Adu33 which states that: the 'presumption' that a claimant's sworn testimony is true is always rebuttable, and , in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention. Thus, the panel concludes that the claimant's testimony in this regard is untrustworthy.

The panel is not persuaded that the claimant travelled to Canada on a holiday and that only after she arrived did she learn that she would be persecuted if she returned to Ethiopia. The timing of events indicates otherwise. The claimant testified that, while she was working in Paris, she received a letter informing her that she XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She provided a copy of a letter from the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris, dated XXXX, 2009.34 The letter states that her presence at her new workplace in Ethiopia is required no later than XXXX, 2009. The claimant testified that the reason she and her husband and daughter travelled to Canada was to enjoy a holiday. The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXX, 2009.35 The claimant testified that, after she had arrived in Canada, she received a warning e-mail36 with an attachment37 from XXX, a friend of a friend in the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX XXXXX. The e-mail was sent XXXX, 2009. The claimant testified that XXX, while working at the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX XXXXX, allegedly came across a private document [the attachment] regarding the claimant from XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant alleges that it is the information in this attachment that caused her to apply for refugee protection. It is not apparent by whom the attached document38 is written or to whom it is sent; it has no heading, salutation or signature; it has no date. Therefore, the panel gives it little weight. The panel finds it more than coincidental that the claimant had a travel visa issued XXXXX, 2009, which she used to travel on a holiday to Canada less than a week before she was required to return to Ethiopia for work, remained in Canada after the required return date to Ethiopia, and then received an e-mail from a friend of a friend she happens to know in the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX XXXXX who saw the report [the e-mail attachment]against the claimant which caused the claimant to make a claim for protection on September 1, 2009. With regard to the coincidences, the panel is guided by the Federal Court decision in Ankrah,39 where J. Noel stated: The applicant's story does otherwise reveal a series of events of chance, and it was open to the tribunal to conclude there from that the Applicant's testimony was too fortuitous in nature to be believed.40

The panel finds the claimant's credibility is diminished due to this testimony. The panel finds that it is not reasonable that the claimant could travel to Canada less than a week before she was required to return to Ethiopia if, as she alleges, she was suspected of opposing the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The claimant testified that she was able to leave France and travel to Canada because she had the appropriate travel visa. When the panel asked the claimant if the XXXXX was aware that she would travel to Canada she testified that it was reasonable that they knew. Given the strict monitoring of Ethiopian citizens, the treatment in particular of those in opposition to the government,41 that the claimant's activities had come under scrutiny by the XXXXX XXXXX 42 and she was required to return to Ethiopia it is not reasonable that she and her immediately family were allowed to travel to Canada less that a week before she was to asked to return to Ethiopia. Thus, the panel finds the claimant's testimony lacks credibility.

The panel is not persuaded that the claimant has good grounds to fear persecution upon return to Ethiopia. The panel believes that the claimant had three people who could have provided evidence for her in this regard but did not. The claimant was asked why XXX, the person who sent the e-mail and attachment,43 could not have provided clear evidence for the claimant. The claimant testified that she had not considered asking her. The claimant was asked why she had not asked her father for evidence. The claimant testified that she didn't think of it. The claimant testified that her former boss, XXX XXXXX, at the office in Paris, knew her father and suspected that she, the claimant, was having problems with authorities at the XXXXX XXXXX. She testified that XXX XXXXX made a claim for asylum in the US. The claimant was asked why XXX XXXXX had not provided evidence for the claimant. She explained that she had not been in contact with him for a long time. The panel does not find the claimant's explanations satisfactory for not obtaining or attempting to obtain evidence from three people whom allegedly knew something of her claim. She was in contact with XXX and her father; XXX XXXXX is in the US where he could possibly have been located. As for the lack of documentation from people who allegedly knew of the claimant's problems with the Ethiopian authorities, the panel finds that the claimant has failed to provide, contrary to her onus to do so, relevant documentation to establish her claim. Rule 744 of the Refugee Protection Division stipulates that the claimant "must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and other elements of the claim." If the claimant does not provide such documents, he/she must be able to explain the reason they were not provided or at least relay what steps were taken to obtain them.45 The panel also refers to the Mohideen Osman decision46 where the Court held that Regarding the failure of the corroborating letters ...where there is no reasonable explanation for material omissions, they can be the basis of an adverse inference and impugn an applicant's credibility.47 The claimant has failed to provide acceptable documents establishing her claim or acceptable reasons for not doing so. The panel finds the claimant not credible.

For a further reason, the panel is not persuaded that the claimant was to be returned to Ethiopia to face persecution. The claimant testified that none of her family or her husband's family suffered harm at the hands of the Ethiopian authorities. The documentary evidence indicates that family members of those who oppose the Ethiopian government are ill-treated and sometimes imprisoned.48 The claimant testified that her family received telephone calls inquiring about her whereabouts and that her mother was questioned at work by the authorities. The panel finds that none of these examples rise to the level of ill-treatment. The claimant testified that the Ethiopian authorities allowed her mother to travel to France when her father became seriously ill in 2010. She testified that her mother is presently in France. The panel believes that it is probable that the claimant's mother was identified as the wife of XXXXX XXXX XXXXX when she was allowed to travel to France. The panel believes that such a repressive regime as that in Ethiopia would not have allowed the claimant's mother to travel outside of the country if the claimant were wanted for serious political opposition activities. The panel finds that the claimant's credibility is further compromised.

The panel does not find it credible that the claimant allowed her infant daughter to return to Ethiopia for six weeks in XXXX 2009 if the claimant was fearful that the Ethiopian authorities believed she opposed them. The claimant testified that it was late in 2005 that officials learned who her father was and that they accused her of being influenced by his political views. She testified that she had problems with officials who were angry with her and told her she was disobedient because she was unwilling to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She stated that she was intimidated and received verbal abuse each time she went to work at the XXXX XXXX. The claimant testified that her husband and daughter returned to Ethiopia in XXXX 2009. She testified that her husband carried her father XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The claimant was asked if she was not concerned for her child's safety in Ethiopian given that the claimant was under suspicion by the authorities and that in her Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative she stated her husband was carrying some of her father's books, writings and CDs to distribute to retail shops in XXXXX XXXXX and its vicinity. The claimant testified that the authorities had a problem with her, not her child. The panel finds that the claimant's evidence became equivocal in nature in an attempt to minimize the information found in her PIF narrative when she referred to the media her husband carried. She testified that her husband visited only one store in XXXXX XXXXX that carries lots of opposition media; she explained that her husband brought only one of her father's books thus she didn't think the authorities would put much pressure on her husband. The claimant was asked if she didn't fear that her husband and daughter might be detained by the XXXXX XXXXX. She testified that she didn't think the Ethiopian government was capable of this and, in any case, her mother-in-law in Ethiopia was desperate to see her granddaughter. The panel does not find the claimant's explanations reasonable. She is well educated.49 Documentary evidence states that the Ethiopian government uses a widespread system of paid informants to report on the activities of individuals and security forces detain family members of those who oppose the government.50 According to her PIF narrative51 and her testimony, she is aware of the political situation in Ethiopia and knowledgeable about her father's experiences with the XXXXX XXXXX. In Paris, from 2005 to 2009, she had been living and working in a XXXXX XXXXXX and the panel infers she would have been made further aware of the situation for those who opposed the Ethiopian government. The panel can appreciate that the principal claimant's mother might wish to see her grandchild but the panel believes that the child's safety would be paramount to the claimant. The panel does not believe that the claimant would have allowed her one year old child to return to Ethiopia if she had personal concerns about the XXXXX XXXXX. Subjective Fear
The panel finds that the claimant's behaviour is not that of a person who is fearful of persecution.

The question of subjective fear is raised when a person voluntarily leaves a country where he or she could safely live or fails without valid reason to ask for protection in a country through which he or she has travelled.52 There is a presumption that persons fleeing persecution will seek protection at the first opportunity, which would normally be in the first country they reach. Failure to seek the protection of another country which is also a signatory of the Convention53 may be a significant factor to consider with regard to subjective fear. France became a signatory of the Convention in 1954. The claimant did not seek protection from the government of France during the more than four years she lived there. In addition to the concerns the claimant had with the XXXXX XXXXX already referred to, the claimant stated that upon her return from a holiday in the United States (US) in 2008 she was interrogated about the purpose of her visit there. She stated that she was suspected of contacting Ethiopian opposition parties in the US. When asked to explain why she did not make a claim in France, the claimant testified that, since she worked for the XXXXX XXXXX, she was afraid that a diplomatic approach might be used to disallow the claim. The claimant provided no persuasive evidence that this might have been the case. Indeed, her father, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, lived safely in the protection of the French government for over thirty years. The panel does not believe that the French government would be persuaded to disallow a refugee claim by diplomatic means. The panel finds that the claimant could have sought the protection of France if she genuinely feared persecution in Ethiopia. In the decision of Safakhoo the Federal Court found that it was inconsistent with a well-founded fear of persecution that the applicants should sojourn in France for five years without making an application for refugee status.54 In the decision of Hibo Farah Mohamed and Ardo Abdi Omer v. MCI, the Court held: The Geneva Convention exists for persons who require protection and not to assist persons who simply prefer asylum in one country over another. The Convention and the Immigration Act should be interpreted with the correct purpose in mind.55 Similarly, in the Case of Assadi, Nasser-Eddin v MCI, the Court held: Failure to immediately seek protection can impugn the claimant's credibility, including his or her testimony about events in his country of origin.56

As stated earlier, the claimant testified that she came under the suspicion of the Ethiopian government not long after she arrived in France in 2005 and suffered verbal abuse and intimidation from that time until mid-2009. The panel determines that the claimant's failure to seek protection in France undermines her subjective fear of persecution.

After considering the claimant's failure to seek protection in France, where the claimant had reasonable opportunity to do so, the panel determines that she has not established a subjective fear of persecution. The Principal Claimant

The panel does not find it credible that the principal claimant returned to Ethiopia for six weeks with his infant in XXXX 2009 and with literature of XXXXX XXXXX if he knew that the claimant was fearful that the XXXXX XXXXX believed she opposed them. The principal claimant testified that he was aware of his wife's problems with the XXXXX XXXXX in Paris. He testified that he carried the political literature of XXXXX XXXXX because he was asked to. The principal claimant was asked why he returned to Ethiopia given his wife's problems. The principal claimant testified that his mother insisted on seeing her grandchild. He further explained that he was not involved in any political activities; he testified that if the authorities in Ethiopia knew of his wife's circumstances he didn't think there would be any difficulties. The panel does not find the principal claimant's explanations reasonable. He is well educated with seventeen years of formal education.57 As stated previously, documentary evidence states that the Ethiopian government uses a widespread system of paid informants to report on the activities of individuals and security forces detain family members of those who oppose the government.58 The principal claimant lived in Paris with his wife and his father-in-law, XXXXX XXXXX, from 2006 to 2009. He was knowledgeable about the problems his wife faced with authorities at the XXXXX XXXXX. The panel can appreciate that the principal claimant's mother might wish to see her grandchild but the panel believes that the child's safety would be vital to the principal claimant. The panel does not believe that the principal claimant would have carried literature opposing the Ethiopian authorities and taken his one year old child to Ethiopia if he was aware of the principal claimant's problems with XXXXX XXXXX. The principal claimant's behaviour is not consistent with that of someone genuinely fearing removal to a place of persecution. The panel finds the principal claimant's testimony in this regard untrustworthy. Conclusion s. 96

After considering all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant is not credible and has, therefore, not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility that she would be persecuted for a Convention ground. The panel is aware that none of the credibility concerns raised here may be sufficient, each on its own, to negate this claim. However, given that these concerns touch upon such important, central issues in the claim, the cumulative effect is that the panel does not have sufficient credible or trustworthy evidence upon which to base a determination that the claimant is a Convention refugee. Section 97(1)
The claimant advanced no persuasive evidence to suggest she would face any danger, that is, more likely than not, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture.

Given the findings above, that the claimant is not a credible witness and lacks subjective fear, the panel finds that she is not a person who faces a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she were to return to Ethiopia.
For these reasons, the claimant is not a person in need of protection.

The claimant, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 96 or subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The principal claimant and the minor claimant depend upon the claim of XXXXX XXXX XXXXX. Therefore, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX XXXX are also not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 96 or subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). (signed) 'L. MASON' L.
